questions.question: What is the difference between var and := in Go?
questions.title: var vs := in Go
questions.direct_answer: var declares a variable and may use an explicit type; := infers the type and is allowed only inside functions. Use := for local values when the type is obvious, and var when you need package scope, a zero value, or an explicit type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know scope and type inference rules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using := at package scope or assuming it redeclares every name.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that at least one name on the left must be new for :=, while an existing variable may be reassigned in the same scope.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define var vs := in Go simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Declaration rules
sections.content: `var` works at package or function scope and can declare a zero value. `:=` is shorthand for declaration plus inference, but only inside a function.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
```go
var retries int
name := "Ada"
retries, name = 2, "Grace"
```

sections.title: Remember
items: Use var for zero values, package variables, or explicit types.
A short declaration must introduce at least one new variable in its scope.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In Go, var is the general declaration form and can be used at package scope, while := is concise type-inferred syntax restricted to function bodies. I choose := for obvious local values and var when I want a zero value or an explicit type.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.

followup_questions: What zero value does an undeclared int receive?
